blocks.text: Nathan’s story of a rich man taking a poor man’s only lamb exposes David’s actions by analogy. When Nathan says, “Thou art the man,” he identifies David as the one who took from Uriah and caused Uriah’s death; the chapter’s judgment is therefore direct, not ambiguous.

A disputed interpretive observation emphasizes the imbalance of royal power in the events Nathan condemns: David summons and takes Bath-sheba while king, then engineers Uriah’s death. On this reading, the narrative should not be softened into a harmless mutual romance, because it presents David’s conduct as condemned wrongdoing.

Second Samuel’s wider movement begins with David’s accession and the consolidation of his kingdom, includes the ark and the promise concerning his dynasty, and then moves through royal abuse, household violence, rebellion, grief, and a closing appendix. Chapter 12 belongs to this larger account of David’s reign rather than standing as an isolated episode.
